title: From model weights to API endpoint with TensorRT LLM: Philip Kiely and Pankaj Gupta
talk_summary: A Base 10 workshop on building and serving TensorRT-LLM engines: converting checkpoints, building engines tuned to GPU/sequence/batch shapes, FP8 quantization, and benchmarking throughput/latency before production. It is almost entirely about self-hosting GPU inference infrastructure, not about agent orchestration or review quality.

takeaways.technique: Benchmark batch-size vs latency tradeoff before picking serving config
takeaways.what_they_do: They run a warm-up then measure time-to-first-token and total tokens/sec at several concurrency levels, noting throughput is non-linear and collapses past a saturation point.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the performance that you get out of your model once it's actually built and deployed is not necessarily just going to be linear
takeaways.numbers: TTFT barely moves 32->64 batch but spikes at 128; total TPS 5,000 at concurrency 32 vs 7,000 at 64 on an A10G

takeaways.technique: FP8 post-training quantization of weights and KV cache
takeaways.what_they_do: They quantize both weights and KV cache to FP8 with a short calibration pass, which roughly halves engine size and unlocks tensor-core speedups, with quality described as near-indistinguishable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: FP8 is about 40% better in most scenarios
takeaways.numbers: Engine size 2GB -> 1.2GB after FP8; ~40% better; calibration takes ~5 minutes

takeaways.technique: Fast parallel downloads for large artifacts (hf_transfer)
takeaways.what_they_do: They use hf_transfer to slice and parallel-download model weights, reaching ~1GB/s, to keep cold starts and setup fast.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it works really, really fast. It goes up to like 1 gig a second

takeaways.what_they_do: Their benchmark script always does a warm-up request before recording numbers so cold-start effects don't pollute results.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Always want to have a warm-up run before you get the real numbers
